title: Finite Element Method
tagline: The direct stiffness method, weak forms and Galerkin's method, frame, plane and isoparametric elements, convergence, field problems, structural dynamics and nonlinear analysis
summary: The finite element method turns the equations of mechanics into matrix problems a computer can solve, and is the main tool for analysing real structures. The course starts from springs, bars and trusses with the direct stiffness method, develops weak forms and Galerkin's method, builds frame, plane and isoparametric elements with numerical integration, studies convergence and meshing, extends the method to heat conduction, vibration and nonlinear problems, and ends with the verification of models.
overview: The finite element method (FEM) replaces a continuous body by a finite number of pieces — elements — joined at nodes, approximates the displacement (or temperature, or potential) inside each piece by simple functions of the nodal values, and turns the differential equations of mechanics into a system of linear or nonlinear algebraic equations $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{F}$. It is the standard tool for stress, vibration and thermal analysis of machine parts, vehicles, aircraft, pressure equipment and buildings, and almost every commercial analysis code is built on the ideas of this course.

The course follows the historical order, which is also the easiest one to learn in. It starts with springs, bars and trusses, where the direct stiffness method — element stiffness, assembly, supports, solution, recovery of stresses — can be done by hand, and adds beam and frame elements. It then puts the method on its proper foundation: the weak form of a boundary-value problem, the principle of virtual work and Galerkin's method, which explain where element matrices come from and why the answers converge. With that foundation the course builds plane triangles and quadrilaterals, isoparametric elements integrated by Gauss quadrature, and studies convergence, locking, stress recovery and meshing.

The last three chapters carry the same machinery to heat conduction and other field problems, to structural dynamics (mass matrices, natural frequencies and time integration), and to nonlinear problems solved by Newton–Raphson iteration, ending with the practice of building, checking and verifying a model. The hard part of the subject is not the algebra, which a computer does, but judgement: knowing what an element can and cannot represent, whether a mesh is fine enough, and whether a coloured stress plot is believable. Every chapter therefore works small problems completely by hand and checks the results against exact solutions, so that you learn what the computer is doing before you trust it with a problem you cannot check.
outcomes: Derive the stiffness matrix of spring, bar, truss, beam and plane-frame elements, assemble them into a global system, apply supports and solve for displacements, member forces and reactions by hand.
Transform element matrices between local and global coordinates for plane and space trusses and frames.
Derive the weak form of a one-dimensional boundary-value problem, distinguish essential from natural boundary conditions, and construct Galerkin and Rayleigh–Ritz approximations.
Formulate constant-strain triangles and bilinear quadrilaterals for plane stress and plane strain, including their B and D matrices and consistent nodal loads.
Map isoparametric elements to their parent domain, compute the Jacobian, and choose a Gauss quadrature rule that is accurate without introducing spurious zero-energy modes.
Estimate discretisation error from a sequence of meshes, recognise locking and stress singularities, and recover improved stresses.
Solve steady and transient heat conduction and other scalar field problems with finite elements, and choose a stable time step.
Compute natural frequencies and mode shapes with consistent and lumped mass matrices, and integrate the equations of motion with the central-difference and Newmark methods.
Solve nonlinear equilibrium problems by Newton–Raphson iteration, recognise limit points and snap-through, and check a finite element model systematically before trusting it.

chapters.title: Springs, bars and the direct stiffness method
chapters.summary: Element stiffness matrices, assembly, boundary conditions and solution for systems of springs and bars.

chapters.title: Trusses and frames
chapters.summary: Truss elements in two and three dimensions, coordinate transformations, and beam and frame elements.

chapters.title: Weak forms and Galerkin's method
chapters.summary: Strong and weak forms, the principle of virtual work, shape functions and Galerkin's method for one-dimensional problems.

chapters.title: Two-dimensional elements
chapters.summary: Constant-strain triangles and bilinear quadrilaterals for plane stress and plane strain.

chapters.title: Isoparametric elements and numerical integration
chapters.summary: Isoparametric mapping and the Jacobian, Gauss quadrature, and higher-order and three-dimensional elements.

chapters.title: Convergence, accuracy and meshing
chapters.summary: Patch tests and rates of convergence, locking, stress recovery, and mesh refinement guided by error estimates.

chapters.title: Heat conduction and other field problems
chapters.summary: Finite elements for steady and transient heat conduction and other scalar field problems, with time integration.

chapters.title: Structural dynamics
chapters.summary: Consistent and lumped mass matrices, modal analysis and direct time integration of structural vibration.

chapters.title: Nonlinear analysis and modelling practice
chapters.summary: Geometric and material nonlinearity solved by Newton–Raphson iteration, and good practice in building, checking and verifying models.

history.title: Hrennikoff's framework method
history.detail: Alexander Hrennikoff modelled plane elastic bodies as lattices of bars and beams whose stiffness mimicked the continuum (*Journal of Applied Mechanics*, 1941) — the structural-engineering root of the method.

history.title: Courant's piecewise-linear triangles
history.detail: Richard Courant solved the torsion problem by minimising its energy over functions that are linear on each triangle of a mesh (*Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society*, 1943) — the mathematical root of the method, unnoticed by engineers for two decades.

history.title: Turner, Clough, Martin and Topp: the direct stiffness method
history.detail: Working on delta-wing structures at Boeing, the four authors derived stiffness matrices for bar and triangular plate elements and assembled them directly ("Stiffness and deflection analysis of complex structures", *Journal of the Aeronautical Sciences*, 1956). Argyris's series "Energy theorems and structural analysis" in *Aircraft Engineering* (1954–55) developed the matrix theory of structures in parallel.

history.title: Newmark's time-integration method
history.detail: Nathan Newmark published "A method of computation for structural dynamics" (*Journal of the Engineering Mechanics Division, ASCE*, 1959); its average-acceleration member is still the default implicit integrator in structural codes.

history.title: Clough names the finite element method
history.detail: In "The finite element method in plane stress analysis", presented at the 2nd ASCE Conference on Electronic Computation in Pittsburgh, Clough derived the constant-strain triangle by virtual work and gave the method its name.

history.title: The first textbook
history.detail: Olgierd Zienkiewicz and Y. K. Cheung published *The Finite Element Method in Structural and Continuum Mechanics* (McGraw-Hill, 1967), which presented the method as a general technique for field problems as well as structures.

history.title: Isoparametric elements
history.detail: Ergatoudis, Irons and Zienkiewicz introduced curved isoparametric quadrilaterals integrated numerically (*International Journal of Solids and Structures*, 1968), building on Irons's 1966 note on numerical integration in stiffness methods; the idea underlies almost every modern continuum element.

history.title: Strang and Fix: the mathematical theory
history.detail: Gilbert Strang and George Fix's *An Analysis of the Finite Element Method* (Prentice-Hall, 1973) established convergence rates and error estimates and made the method a branch of numerical analysis.

history.title: A posteriori error estimation
history.detail: Zienkiewicz and Zhu proposed estimating the error of a solution by comparing its stresses with smoothed ones (*International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering*, 1987), the basis of adaptive meshing in commercial codes; their superconvergent patch recovery followed in 1992.

history.title: The loss of Sleipner A
history.detail: The concrete gravity base of the Sleipner A platform sank during a ballast test in a Norwegian fjord in August 1991. The investigation traced the failure of a tricell wall to a finite element analysis that underestimated the shear in the wall by about 45 %, partly through poorly shaped elements, together with inadequate reinforcement — a lasting lesson in checking models.

references.authors: R. D. Cook, D. S. Malkus, M. E. Plesha and R. J. Witt
references.title: Concepts and Applications of Finite Element Analysis
references.note: 4th edition, Wiley. The clearest engineering introduction, strong on element behaviour, modelling and error; the closest match to this course.

references.title: A First Course in the Finite Element Method
references.note: 6th edition, Cengage. Many fully worked hand calculations for springs, bars, trusses, beams, frames and plane elements.

references.title: A First Course in Finite Elements
references.note: Wiley. A compact, modern treatment built on weak forms from the start.

references.title: The Finite Element Method: Linear Static and Dynamic Finite Element Analysis
references.note: Dover reprint of the 1987 Prentice-Hall book. Rigorous on variational formulation, isoparametric elements and time integration.

references.title: Finite Element Procedures
references.note: 2nd edition (1st edition Prentice Hall, 1996). The standard reference for the solution algorithms: equation solvers, eigensolvers, time integration and nonlinear iteration.

references.authors: O. C. Zienkiewicz, R. L. Taylor and J. Z. Zhu
references.title: The Finite Element Method: Its Basis and Fundamentals
references.note: 7th edition, Butterworth-Heinemann. The classic encyclopaedic text, including field problems, patch tests and error estimation.

references.authors: G. Strang and G. J. Fix
references.title: An Analysis of the Finite Element Method
references.note: Prentice-Hall (2nd edition, Wellesley-Cambridge, 2008). The mathematical theory of convergence for readers who want proofs.

references.title: Non-Linear Finite Element Analysis of Solids and Structures, Volume 1: Essentials
references.note: Wiley. Newton–Raphson and arc-length methods explained through small truss examples.
